articles.title: Protesters testing maximum tolerance limits during ASEAN, says PNP
articles.summary: The statement follows the arrest of hundreds of activists over the ASEAN Summit weekend, including 200 anti-Pax Silica protesters in Muntinlupa.

blocks.text: November 16, 2026 | 5:43pm

Protesters clash with police officers during a demonstration that coincides with the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Leaders' Summit and Related Summits in Manila on Nov. 15, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police (PNP) warned protesters Monday, November 16, not to "mistake maximum tolerance and restraint for weakness" as it defended police operations that led to hundreds of arrests during the opening weekend of the ASEAN summit.

PNP spokesperson Allen Rae Co denied that police had barred activists from approaching summit venues in Pasay City, saying officers had exercised restraint despite confrontations that left several police personnel injured.
Co also denied that police instigated a confrontation with protesters opposing the US-led Pax Silica initiative in Sucat, Muntinlupa City, where more than 200 people were arrested.
"We negotiated for 12 hours in Muntinlupa. We asked them to clear the road because no one could pass, but they insisted on going. Isn't marching part of protesting?" Co said.
He described the protesters' blockade as a "disruption" and questioned the groups' intentions.
Co argued that protest organizations forfeited their right to peaceful assembly when their objective was to "create maximum disturbance and inconvenience to others."
Progressive groups, however, estimated that more than 300 people had been arrested in connection with demonstrations during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit.
Police respond to harassment claims
Co also addressed reports of police harassment of journalists covering the demonstrations, saying the incidents were unintentional.

"We understand, of course, that you are journalists, and you are bound by duty to report what is happening to the public. But during these times, if your positioning or actions are unclear, and you act as if you're part of the protestors … our officers were injured," Co said.
Journalists covering the protests have reported harassment by police, raising concerns over their ability to document the demonstrations.
Human rights watchdog Amnesty International Philippines called for the immediate and unconditional release of the arrested protesters in a statement Sunday.

articles.title: Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
articles.summary:
Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China efforts to dominate

Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a…

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.

The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.

Underlying the diplomatic swing are efforts by the federal government to avoid angering China, as the Quad leaders gather for the first time since 2024 - and after Australia joined countries, including the US and Japan, in an agreement for new protections around key AI technologies.

Designed to firm up supply chains for chips and critical minerals components, the San Francisco Declaration was crafted to promote cooperation in the face of China’s efforts to control areas of AI development.

Part of the Pax Silica international accord, officials said the agreement would help ensure Trump worked with partners to set standards in AI, rather than relying on others for leadership. Signatories including the UK, India, Israel, South Korea and Singapore.
Albanese told the Asean-Australia summit on Monday that the region needed friendship, mutual trust, and optimism to prosper.
“At a time of global instability, the cooperation we demonstrate here will help us to confront the challenges we share at home and in our region,” he said.

Federal government sources told Guardian Australia the intense international efforts, including Albanese’s attendance at the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China at the end of the week, was about maintaining engagement with Trump in the final two years of his presidency and stopping the US from withdrawing from global leadership.

Asia Society senior fellow Premesha Saha said the Quad talks would focus on critical minerals, maritime security and energy security. Albanese and Trump will be joined by Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi and India’s Narendra Modi would discuss

“For Australia, keeping the United States engaged in the Indo-Pacific is a core strategic interest, and the Quad is one of the few settings where the president is tied into a regional agenda alongside three close partners,” Saha said.
“After a year in which Washington has been engaged elsewhere and has opened its own channel with Beijing, getting Trump to a Quad leaders’ meeting in the region matters to Australia.”
Saha said Albanese’s objectives included keeping Washington engaged in the region and building a Quad capable of delivering results, even during shifts in US policy and interest.
“Beijing will criticise it, as it always does, and will cast it as bloc politics. But I will be cautious about overstating how much this will anger China,” she said.
“The Quad isn’t a military alliance, and Washington has gone out of its way to say it isn’t an anti-China coalition.”
Jennifer Parker, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, said criticism of Albanese’s involvement in the annual international summit season was shortsighted.
“Our relationships in the region are essential to our security in an increasingly chaotic world, and our security is the backbone of our national prosperity,” she said.
“It is important for Australia to be seen on the international stage and advocate for our national interests.”
after newsletter promotion
Parker disagreed that Australia was working to keep the US engaged in the Asia Pacific region.
“The US has enduring interests here, both economically and strategically. But sometimes it pays for Australia to remind them of that,” she said.
Albanese announced a new Asean–Australia digital economy program on Monday, to support AI safety and intelligence standards and digital trade standards.
He said humans must remain in control of AI, shaping the technology “rather than let it shape us.”
Albanese also held one-on-one talks with Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

He told his Laos counterpart, Saleumxay Kommasith, that Australia remained very concerned about the deaths of backpackers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vientiane in 2024.
Albanese said Australia remained concerned about the seriousness of charges over the deaths. Investigators said they did not have enough evidence to do more because autopsies were not carried out.
Albanese called the case a “tragedy” and said it remained a serious issue in Australia.
Kommasith said the Laos government had attached importance to the case and officials were “trying our best to to put an end to this by bringing those perpetrators into justice”.

articles.title: ASEAN, Australia eye stronger trade, maritime security
articles.summary: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and Australia on Monday committed to strengthening two-way trade and investment and continuing cooperation on maritime security.

blocks.text: Published November 16, 2026 5:34pm
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and Australia on Monday committed to strengthening two-way trade and investment and continuing cooperation on maritime security.

During the 6th ASEAN-Australia Summit, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. said Australia, ASEAN's first dialogue partner, had long supported the region's efforts to advance peace, prosperity and sustainable development.
“Our cooperation spans maritime security, cybersecurity, counterterrorism, and the fight against trafficking in persons, online scams, and illicit drugs,” Marcos said.
The President also highlighted the growing economic ties between ASEAN and Australia.
“Two-way trade reached AUD197.5 billion last year, and the upgraded ASEAN-Australia-New Zealand Free Trade Area gives our businesses greater market access and certainty,” Marcos said.
He also noted Australia's commitment of up to AUD15 million (about P648.2 million) for the ASEAN Centre for Public Health Emergencies and Emerging Diseases.

Marcos said Australia also supports the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance on Disaster Management, the new TRIANGLE Partnerships for migrant workers, and Timor-Leste's integration into ASEAN.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, meanwhile, vowed to continue investing in ASEAN and ASEAN-led institutions.

“Because we believe in ASEAN centrality and that this is the key to our region's success and our shared future. And because as a reliable partner, we understand that maintaining peace and stability in our region is a collective responsibility,” Albanese said.

“Together, we recommit our efforts to increasing our two-way trade and investment, harnessing the opportunities of clean energy, climate resilience, better infrastructure, fairer educational opportunities and strengthened maritime security,” he added.
Albanese said shared security and peace depended on shared economic prosperity, adding that Australia aimed to deepen its economic ties with its regional partners.
He cited Australia's Southeast Asia Economic Strategy to 2040, which he said had supported $4.5 billion in new Australian investments in ASEAN.

“We are determined to keep building on this progress and today I announce also that we will expand our investment deal teams and establish a new Invested 2040 window through Australian Development Investments, our international impact investment fund,” he said.
“These initiatives will connect Australian capital with Southeast Asia's fastest growing businesses, helping us to harness the region's next wave of economic growth,” he added.

Albanese also expressed confidence that ASEAN and Australia could continue responding to global conflicts and challenges, including the oil and energy crisis, by investing in the resilience of their shared energy supply chains.— MCG, GMA News

blocks.text: The report paints a picture of the Philippines as wanting to adopt AI to have a competitive advantage, even as it deals with being about two years behind the global AI maturity curve

items: The Philippine AI Maturity Report highlights the country's ambition to adopt AI for competitive advantage, despite being behind the global maturity curve.
Philippine companies face challenges in talent, data, and execution, which could hinder their ability to leverage AI effectively.
To succeed in AI adoption, collaboration between government and businesses is essential to address structural barriers and enhance organizational capabilities.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Artificial intelligence will change the direction of the labor-driven model of the Philippines, but how its changes will impact the country will depend on how companies respond to and invest in AI.

Boston Consulting Group collaborated with the Makati Business Club to release The Philippine AI Maturity Report last Wednesday, November 11. The report paints a picture of the Philippines as wanting to adopt AI to have a competitive advantage, even as the country deals with being about two years behind the global AI maturity curve.
While Philippine companies hold big ambitions for AI — with more than half aiming to reach the highest level of maturity by 2029 — gaps in talent, data, and execution continue holding back potential.

The report noted how Philippine labor cost is 70% below the Asia-Pacific average and 80% below the global average. The problem, however, is if demand for this labor will continue to be maintained in an age where some Philippine labor tasks are being offloaded to AI.

Said the report, “Many of the leading AI-native players emerged only after 2022, yet some have already reached significant scale with relatively small teams. As these technologies mature, firms in high-cost markets gain both a more viable alternative to offshoring routine work and a model for delivering services with fewer people.”

The report envisions two possible scenarios for the Philippines: either AI automates the work on which the Philippines currently competes for, eroding the traditional cost advantage, or AI augments the workforce and allows the Philippines to compete on capability rather than cost alone.

Currently, the report noted we are closer to the former scenario rather than the latter. It is suggested that, in light of the two possible scenarios, “Philippine firms have to overinvest in AI to become competitive in the regional landscape.”

The Philippines is playing catch-up to the global trajectory of AI use and adoption, with the country’s 2026 average maturity remaining closer to the global average from 2024 than to the global average today.
The report explained that “AI maturity is advancing quickly, and the benefits are increasingly accruing to companies that can move from experimentation to scaled, enterprise-wide adoption.”

Companies in the Philippines are thus working on embracing and adapting to AI at a rapid pace, with companies having three-year targets aiming for an average maturity increase of roughly 34 percentage points, or about 11 points per year. This is around 2.5x the actual pace of improvement recently observed in the global average.
As such, Philippine companies are ambitiously setting sights on what the report termed as “a major step-change in AI maturity” by 2029.
To that end, the report cites the weakest link that needs to be addressed: the people factor.

The report noted a gap between the building of AI capabilities versus how well AI capabilities are embedded into a given organization. The ways in which people work will help determine if AI is used properly and creates value for organizations.

“The next phase of AI maturity for the Philippines will therefore depend less on adding more foundations and more on activating them across people, processes, and ways of working so that existing AI capabilities translate into tangible business outcomes,” the report said.
The report also said Philippine companies invest in line with peers in IT and IT-based AI, but said that “greater value lies in non-IT AI to support business transformation, not just cost reduction.”
The report also emphasized three bottlenecks the Philippines has to deal with as it seeks to better get a handle on AI:

items: When it comes to data, companies lacking the integrated and usable data foundation needed to scale AI.
When it comes to talent, the country’s talent system does not yet consistently produce and retain the advanced skills AI requires.
When it comes to cost, Philippine companies face a tougher economic equation: they pay close to global prices for AI while operating against a lower local cost base.

blocks.text: Accordingly, the report concludes that if we want to take higher-value path in adopting and thriving in the AI-enabled future, we will need government and business to move and work together “to address the structural barriers to AI adoption while building the organizational capabilities needed to turn AI into sustained business value.”

To do this, the report suggests the government should address the bottlenecks by connecting fragmented data and digitizing Philippine business activity for AI, by building talent and providing Philippine talent convincing reasons to stay, and creating conditions to make AI affordable in the Philippines.
Meanwhile, it also recommended businesses do the following:

items: Set a focused, multiyear AI agenda with clear business outcomes
Pick a few strategic outcomes and win them
Focus on upskilling and transforming your people
Continue investing in the technology and data foundation
Be conscious of your tokens’ return on investment
Set up a tracking mechanism for AI impact but leave room for experimentation

articles.title: N.L.’s top-billing doctor faces malpractice lawsuits from 2 former patients
articles.summary: The ophthalmologist who was Newfoundland and Labrador's top-billing doctor for the last two years straight is being sued by two former patients, including one who says his right eye was completely…

image.caption: Ophthalmologist Dr. Harry Dang, who billed MCP more than $4 million in each of the last two years, is facing malpractice lawsuits brought by two former patients in St. John’s, N.L. (Harry Dang/LinkedIn)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

The ophthalmologist who was Newfoundland and Labrador's top-billing doctor for the last two years straight is being sued by two former patients, including one who says his right eye was completely blinded during a botched cataract surgery.
Lawyer for Dr. Harry Dang says ophthalmologist will fight allegations

The ophthalmologist who was Newfoundland and Labrador top-billing doctor for the last two years straight is being sued by two former patients, including one who says his right eye was completely blinded during a botched cataract surgery.
The other ex-patient is accusing Dr. Harry Dang of performing a similar cataract procedure without taking into account an eye condition that rendered the surgery both futile and dangerous.
Dang, whose medical licence was suspended in December 2025 for unknown reasons, is rejecting the allegations, which haven’t been proven in court.

“We are defending these allegations and putting the plaintiffs to the required standard of proof,” said Dang’s lawyer Robin Cook in an email Wednesday declining an interview request on behalf of his client.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Newfoundland and Labrador is neither commenting on Dang’s suspension nor the lawsuits against him. The Jackman Eye Institute, where Dang worked until his suspension, also declined to comment.

items: N.L.'s top-billing doctor suspended by provincial regulator

blocks.text: The first suit against Dang was filed by St. John’s resident Lloyd Janes last June. Janes is also suing the Jackman clinic.
The Jackman Eye Institute on Newfoundland Drive in St. John's, N.L., on Nov. 13, 2026. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)
According to a statement of claim filed in Supreme Court, during a cataract surgery in February 2025, Dang struck Janes’s right eye in an area with a high concentration of blood vessels.

Despite “diligent medical follow-up,” Janes “remains completely blind in his right eye and has been advised by medical care providers that this loss of vision is permanent,” reads the eight-page statement of claim, which adds that subsequent “corrective procedures” proved unsuccessful.

According to the same document, Janes’s left eye already had reduced vision and the surgery therefore had a significant effect on his mobility and health, making it “necessary to rely on family members and other individuals for daily assistance.”
Janes declined an interview request through his lawyer Ken Mahoney.
Second suit
The second former patient, Pierre Kusters, filed his own lawsuit against Dang earlier this fall, on Sept. 25.

Kusters’s statement of claim alleges he underwent a barrage of pre-surgery tests in June 2025, but was never informed of the results. His left eye was operated on two and a half months later. Ever since, he says his vision in that eye has been blurrier than it was before the cataract procedure, according to the document.

Pierre Kusters, a local cellist, underwent a cataract surgery performed by Dr. Harry Dang in September 2025. He says he can no longer drive at night and can no longer read most of his sheet music. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)

Kusters alleges three months after the surgery, and a few days after Dang’s licence was suspended, another ophthalmologist at the Jackman clinic told him the preliminary tests he underwent before the procedure showed he had a pre-existing degenerative eye condition called Fuchs dystrophy.

The disease affects the innermost layer of the cornea and makes cataract surgery ineffectual if the patient doesn’t also receive a cornea transplant at the same time, Kusters said in an interview with Radio-Canada.

"Dr. [Chris] Jackman confirmed that the finding was present in the tests and scans taken on June 25, 2025, prior to the plaintiff's cataract surgery. This was not known to the plaintiff and was not mentioned by the defendant in the pre-surgery consultation,” reads Kusters’s statement of claim. “Individuals with Fuchs dystrophy are not eligible for cataract surgery as they do not properly heal.”

“I’m a bit shaken by it all,” said Kusters, a cellist with the Newfoundland Symphony Orchestra who can no longer read most of his sheet music. He said since the surgery, he can no longer drive at night and moved from Conception Bay South to Mount Pearl in the last month in order to have access to public transit.
Dr. Harry Dang hasn’t practised at the Jackman Eye Clinic since December 2025, when his licence was suspended. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)
Like Janes, Kusters’s vision in his other eye is very weak. He is now waiting for two cornea transplants, a procedure for which there is a five-year waitlist in Newfoundland and Labrador.

“I’d would have liked to have known from the beginning, back in September 2025, that I had this disease. I’d been on a waitlist and maybe today I’d already have been operated on,” said Kusters, who is currently trying to book a surgery in Nova Scotia, where the waitlist for cornea transplants is significantly shorter.

“It’s like Alice in Wonderland. We’ve gone down this rabbit hole and we don’t know how we got there,” said Kusters, who has also filed a formal complaint against Dang with the College of Physicians and Surgeons.
Matthew Head, the CEO of the Jackman clinic, said he couldn’t provide “patient-specific commentary.”
“This matter is still with the legal and regulatory bodies,” Head wrote in an email on Nov. 8.
Dang billed $4M to MCP in each of last 2 years
In 2024-25 and again in 2025-26, despite his suspension with nearly four months left in the fiscal year, Dang was Newfoundland and Labrador’s top-billing doctor.
In 2025-26, he billed $4.25 million to MCP. The year prior, $4.91 million.

In an email Thursday, Donna Walsh of the College of Physicians and Surgeons wrote the organization was unable to comment on any physician or complaint “to ensure that any investigation and/or subsequent hearing is conducted in a fair and impartial manner.”
The regulator wouldn’t say whether Dang’s suspension beyond its current expiration date of Jan. 14, when all annual licences to practice medicine expire and must be renewed.
Dang has not filed a statement of defence in either action. The Jackman clinic also hasn’t filed a statement of defence in the Janes' suit.

articles.title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado
articles.summary:
Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark…

blocks.text: The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.

India’s meteorological department has released an alert for a depression located in the Bay of Bengal with the potential to develop into a cyclone. A low-pressure system formed during the early hours of Friday before developing into a depression on Sunday. The department’s forecast is for the depression to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Tuesday before gradually drifting north-west towards eastern India, with the expectation it will make landfall on Thursday. If the storm were to develop it would become the third of the season and be named Akvan. There is a “watch” level warning for much of the eastern coast on Wednesday and Thursday, with parts of the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha states on an “alert” level.

articles.title: Dismissed Laguna mayor faces graft, unlawful appointment cases
articles.summary: The Ombudsman has ordered criminal charges filed against dismissed Luisiana, Laguna Mayor Jomapher Uy Alvarez over two separate cases.

blocks.text: November 16, 2026 | 5:11pm
Dismissed Luisiana, Laguna Mayor Jomapher Uy Alvarez as seen in a photo posted in 2022.
Alvarez via FB

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman has ordered criminal charges filed against dismissed Luisiana, Laguna Mayor Jomapher Uy Alvarez over the withholding of benefits from former municipal officials and the appointment of an unqualified municipal administrator.
In a statement Monday, November 16, the Ombudsman said it found grounds to charge Alvarez with graft and unlawful appointment under Article 244 of the Revised Penal Code.

The Ombudsman also found Alvarez administratively liable for grave misconduct and violating Section 5 of Republic Act 10154, imposing a dismissal penalty even though he had already been removed from office in an earlier case.
Withheld benefits. The graft case stemmed from a complaint filed by former municipal officials Nestor Alcala Rondilla and Ness Rondilla, whose three-year terms ended on June 30, 2022.
The complainants accused Alvarez of refusing to release their year-end bonuses and cash gifts despite their entitlement to the benefits.
Alvarez denied the allegations, claiming the complaint was politically motivated and that he had never received the letters requesting the release of the funds.
The Ombudsman rejected his defense as self-serving and unsupported by evidence.
It found Alvarez administratively liable for grave misconduct and violating Section 5 of RA 10154, which governs the timely release of retirement benefits.

Although Alvarez had already been dismissed from service following an earlier complaint filed by Rondilla, the Ombudsman imposed another dismissal penalty and ordered the continued enforcement of its accessory penalties.
Unlawful appointment

In a separate case, the Ombudsman ordered Alvarez charged under Article 244 of the Revised Penal Code for appointing Emmanuel Babaan Villamin as municipal administrator in 2022 despite his failure to meet the position's qualifications.

According to the Ombudsman, the municipal government advertised the position with requirements including a college degree, first-grade Civil Service Commission (CSC) eligibility and at least three years of management and administrative experience.
Less than a month later, Alvarez signed Villamin's appointment despite his failure to meet the requirements.
The CSC formally disapproved the appointment in March 2023, prompting Villamin to step down.

Alvarez and municipal human resource management officer I Liza Ludovice Oblenida argued that their roles in the appointment process were merely recommendatory, as the CSC had final authority to approve or reject appointments.
The Ombudsman rejected their defense, stressing that the mayor's appointing authority under the Local Government Code carries a legal responsibility to ensure compliance with civil service rules.

"Respondent Alvarez cannot feign ignorance of the lack of qualifications of respondent Villamin because aside from knowing the latter personally, the basic requirements for the position are spelled out in the job portal, as embodied in Section 480 of the LGC, which respondent Alvarez ought to know," the Ombudsman's decision read.
In the administrative aspect of the appointment case, the Ombudsman imposed a separate suspension of one month and one day without pay on Alvarez.
Oblenida was also given the same suspension after being found administratively liable for simple neglect of duty.

The Ombudsman said the suspensions would be converted into fines equivalent to the respondents' salaries for the same period if they could no longer be enforced because of separation from government service.

articles.title: #CourageON: As COP31 continues, young advocates hope the world will listen
articles.summary: Although not in Antalya, Franciene Enriquez and Mak Bogabong are still keeping an eye on the negotiations, watching out for decisions that could impact their communities

blocks.text: As world leaders and negotiators gather in Antalya, Turkey, for the annual United Nations climate talks, climate advocate Franciene Enriquez hopes someone there is listening.

The negotiations, which began on November 9, are taking place amid wars and growing concerns over fossil fuel dependence. While the energy crisis has renewed arguments for shifting to cheaper clean energy, fossil fuel interests continue to influence the talks.
Civil society organizations and climate advocates are also using the conference to campaign, rally, and press governments to act, bringing the stories of affected communities into the discussions.

While Franciene won’t be attending COP31, she’s waiting for these calls to be actually heard. “We’ve been here for a long, long time…. Hindi kami nabibigyan ng liwanag (We are not being given a chance to be seen).”
Franciene is the founder of Kabataan para sa Kalikasan ng Atimonan and a climate advocate and community facilitator with the Philippine Movement for Climate Justice.

Growing up in Atimonan, Quezon province, she saw how energy development affected communities around her: large trucks interrupting children’s play, families being displaced, dark patches appearing in the sea, and mountains being cut open.

These experiences pushed her to organize against destructive projects, including the proposed Atimonan One Energy coal-fired power plant. In a feature in November 2025, we told Franciene’s story of championing renewable energy, alongside the stories of fellow climate advocates Joshua Villalobos and Mak Bogabong. In the same month, we also wrote about how communities opposed the proposed Atimonan coal plant.
Now in her early twenties, Franciene feels frustrated that her community’s concerns and stories remain in the dark, even after more than 30 years of annual climate negotiations.

“Nakakainis lang, nakakagalit, nakakadismaya kung bakit kapag may mga ganitong usapin lang siya na-bi-bring up (It’s frustrating, infuriating, and disappointing that these issues are only brought up during discussions like COP).”

For Franciene, what happens on the ground is not given enough attention. Speaking out about it, however, comes with risks, including being hunted down or red-tagged. She sees this as part of a wider conflict: companies profit from coal projects, while communities bear their consequences.

On Mak’s side of the country, it’s quite a different story. He is based in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, where awareness of climate change and international climate talks like COP remains limited. Much of his work begins with reaching out to communities and getting them involved in conversations about the climate crisis.

blocks.caption: REPRESENTATION. Mak Bogabong is the sole representative from BARMM at the Mindanao Stakeholders’ Consultation for the Philippines’ Just Transition Framework held in Davao City on September 25-26, 2025. Photo from DENR

blocks.text: Mak is part of JetX Bangsamoro under Reboot Philippines, a youth-led organization advocating for a just transition to renewable energy. He’s also part of ILAYA, or Intergenerational Leaders Advancing Youth for Climate Action, which brings together not just young people but also older generations to work on environmental and climate issues.
“We’re trying to embrace everyone in this advocacy,” Mak said. He shared, with a wide grin, how ILAYA has grown from three members to 15, with a new batch expected to bring its numbers past 20.

ILAYA has organized activities bringing together grade school and high school students to discuss climate change and its effects. Mak was struck by how they responded, even with limited prior knowledge.
“When faced with reality that is inevitable, a reality that is there, a reality that has something to do with your life and death, these young people, the way they think, it’s just amazing,” he said.

blocks.caption: CLIMATE IMMERSION. Mak Bogabong engages in discussions on renewable energy and just transition with Bulacan residents during Reboot Philippines’ immersion activity. Photo from Reboot Philippines

blocks.text: He believes civil society organizations like JetX Bangsamoro can help harness young people’s energy and give them opportunities to act. He won’t be attending COP31 himself, but he hopes the conference will create more opportunities for these groups to participate in climate discussions and decisions.

He also recognizes that political power shapes COP, yet he wants to remain hopeful. “I don’t really have a choice but to be really hopeful,” he said. “A little bit cynical, still…. I want to put myself in the position to remain hopeful.”

Franciene shared that sentiment. The young people in her community often look to her for answers, and she feels she has to keep going for their sake. Although not in Antalya, both she and Mak are still keeping an eye on the negotiations, watching out for decisions that could impact their communities.

blocks.caption: GLIMMERS OF HOPE. Franciene Enriquez speaks with members of KAPAKANAN during a group discussion. Photo by Franciene Enriquez

blocks.text: “I have to be optimistic,” Franciene said. “Kasi, if hindi, anong mangyayari (Because if I’m not, what’s going to be the result of that)?”

“Kailangan mo dito ng malakas na loob (You need courage to do this),” she added. “Wala man akong maayos na sagot na makuha from them (Even if I don’t get a proper answer from the climate negotiations), I will push through to have that answer that I’m seeking.” – Rappler.com

#CourageON is a bi-monthly newsletter providing updates from our communities. In time for the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31), the month of November features stories of courage and resilience from our partner communities and advocates.

articles.title: CBSA demoting border officers who permanently lost ability to use sidearm
articles.summary: The Canada Border Services Agency has informed 63 employees that they will have to take on new, lower-paid positions because of medical conditions that prevent them from carrying a sidearm.

image.caption: A Canada Border Services Agency officer investigates a vehicle in this file photo. The agency has told 63 officers that they will be demoted because of medical issues preventing them from carrying a firearm. (Aaron Lynett/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The Canada Border Services Agency has informed 63 employees that they will have to take on new, lower-paid positions because of medical conditions that prevent them from carrying a sidearm.
Union says officers still have value, agency points to responsible use of public funds
The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) has informed 63 employees that they will have to take on new, lower-paid positions because of medical conditions that prevent them from carrying a sidearm.
The agency told CBC News in a statement that it is willing to offer temporary accommodations to employees who are unable to carry a firearm because of medical or psychological conditions.
However, when employees require permanent accommodation, it said they must be transferred "to a position for which carrying a firearm is not a condition of employment."
Several employees and their union are denouncing the planned demotions, saying that the affected border officers carry out duties that do not require the use of a firearm on a daily basis.

They also say the agency is penalizing experienced employees because of medical or psychological conditions, such as workplace injuries or mental and physical health issues that prevent them from requalifying for firearm use every two years.
The 63 officers affected by the measure represent 0.7 per cent of the 8,500 CBSA positions that require the ability to wear a sidearm.
Union calls process discriminatory, unfair
In a recent message to the employees, the CBSA warned that they would have to go through a "downward deployment without salary protection" as part of the "reasonable accommodation process."
"We think it's discriminatory, it's arbitrary and it's unfair," said Mark Weber, president of the Customs and Immigration Union.
One of the affected officers criticized the message as bureaucratic and impersonal.
Mark Weber is the president of the Customs and Immigration Union. He says the CBSA's decision is discriminatory. (Simon Lasalle/Radio-Canada)
"I felt like a file being closed, not a human being," the employee said.
The officer said they cried when they received the message telling them they would be getting a pay cut after years of service.
"The firearm never helped me do that job. My experience did. That experience didn’t disappear when I stopped being able to carry my gun," they said.
"I want to keep doing work that is important. I’m asking to be able to do that without being punished financially for having a medical disability."
The employee spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss their personal situation without their employer's permission.
In addition to the 63 officers being demoted, 14 employees on sick leave remain under review.
Another 36 officers have retired since January rather than lose the accommodations that allowed them to work in their current roles.

items: Record amounts of Canadian cannabis seized as smuggling to Europe soars

blocks.text: In all, 190 employees had been receiving workplace accommodations related to firearms. Aside from those facing demotion or who have already left, 27 were transferred to positions at the same level and 50 returned to their regular duties after receiving medical clearance.
The CBSA has 18,000 employees, including roughly 8,500 in front-line positions that require carrying a firearm, notably at border crossings and other ports of entry.
Dangerous work at CBSA includes intercepting illegal drugs, firearms and other prohibited goods at the border, as well as deporting individuals who are not authorized to be in Canada.
The use of force remains rare, with CBSA officers across the country drawing their sidearms an average total of 28 times a year.
Several employees who have been granted accommodations related to the carrying of firearms perform office work. (Radio-Canada)

In certain workplaces such as airports and postal centres, border services officers do not always carry their sidearm. Officers can also perform duties without carrying a gun, including working on the Nexus program, analyzing flight manifests and training new officers, according to the union.
A CBSA spokesperson said that "carrying protective and defensive equipment is intrinsically linked to the performance of duties" of border officers, including enforcing the law "when necessary."
"When an individual can no longer be fully armed or meet the requirements of their duties, the CBSA has a duty to accommodate them," said spokesperson Kelly Cameron.

However, she added the agency must spend public funds judiciously and ensure its employees meet the "essential requirements" of positions, including those that require being staffed by an armed officer.
"The CBSA is not required to permanently exempt an employee from performing the essential duties of their position or to create work that is not necessary," she said.

items: The U.S. put surveillance drones in the Great Lakes, and this border town mayor isn't happy

blocks.text: In its letter to the 63 employees who are still unable to carry a firearm, the CBSA stated that there are "no longer any suitable placement opportunities" at their current level.
At least one letter said that available placements would be shared "in the coming weeks."
Weber said the agency is needlessly depriving itself of long-serving employees with decades of experience.
"Essentially, they are being told by their employer that they no longer have value simply because they can no longer carry a firearm," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Daniel Leblanc is a reporter with more than 20 years experience in investigative journalism and federal politics. He is a past winner of the Michener Award, the Charles Lynch Award and three National Newspaper Awards.

articles.title: What will it take for the world's superpowers to agree on AI regulations in war?
articles.summary: As the UN prepares to discuss autonomous weapons this week, insiders say hopes of meaningful, binding regulations around AI in warfare are slim — and time may be running out.

image.caption: Ukrainian servicemen from the special police unit Hyzhak prepare a Gara, a Ukrainian multifunctional unmanned aerial vehicle equipped with AI elements, in the Donetsk region of Ukraine in May. UN diplomats will meet next week in Switzerland to discuss AI use in war. (Anatolii Stepanov/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
As the UN prepares to discuss autonomous weapons this week, insiders say hopes of meaningful, binding regulations around AI in warfare are slim — and time may be running out.
Diplomats to discuss autonomous weapons at a UN meeting this week, but experts say binding rules are unlikely

Diplomats will discuss lethal autonomous weapons systems, including a possible framework for regulations, at a Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons meeting running Monday to Friday in Geneva, Switzerland. More than 100 countries that are party to the convention will be represented, including Canada, the U.S., Russia and China.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned in August that the world was nearing a "moral red line" where autonomous weapons like AI-powered drones could kill without human involvement. He's said he wants a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons by the end of 2026 as AI increasingly becomes a factor in deadly strikes.
Meanwhile, some experts say the use of AI to determine where and when to strike in the first place is an even more pressing concern than the weapons themselves.
But so far, the world's biggest military superpowers — including the U.S., Russia and China — have shot down any serious attempts at binding rules.

items: The age of AI warfare has dawned. Is Canada ready?
Military commander vows fast action on AI and robots, sees 'untapped potential' for Canada

blocks.text: Leaders are afraid of losing their competitive advantage because of the idea that "whoever wins the AI race will dominate the world," said Paul Lushenko, a senior fellow at Cornell University Tech Policy Institute and a retiring U.S. military officer.

He says everyone he speaks to in the military recognizes the moral implications of AI. At the same time, the prevailing consensus among the most powerful militaries is that even if they follow a set of rules, they can't trust their competitors to do the same, creating a Cold War-esque stalemate.
"That's a really challenging position to be in," he said.

Paul Lushenko, senior fellow at Cornell University Tech Policy Institute, says the world's military superpowers worry that if they follow regulations around AI, their competitors won't do the same. (Lisa Maco/Cornell University)
Lushenko said he does not expect any kind of "bona fide international policy" or regulation to come out of this week's meetings.

About one-third of the countries that attended a February military AI summit in Spain, including Canada, agreed to a declaration on how to govern use of the technology in warfare, but the U.S. and China were among those that opted out.
UN diplomats were negotiating a treaty in September to regulate the use of lethal autonomous weapons when U.S. and Russian diplomats cut out key safety provisions on the final day.

According to reporting by the Washington Post, those provisions included language that would have required systems to operate in a predictable and reliable manner, mandated ethical considerations and required that humans review military targets picked by AI before striking.
AI in action
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, addressing the UN in September, warned there is a "real possibility" that AI will soon begin to decide what happens on the battlefield.
"We need peace before we reach that point," he said.

Ukraine and Russia are both increasingly using AI to gain advantages in battle as the war between the two countries approaches its fifth year. In August, the New York Times reported that a Russian drone operated entirely by AI killed three Ukrainian civilians.

items: Israel accused of using AI to choose Gaza targets
Drones and AI are rewriting the rulebook on naval warfare — with uncertain consequences

blocks.text: In one of the most prominent examples of AI-assisted targeting, Israeli intelligence officers described to Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine and the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call how the military's Lavender AI system allegedly identified 37,000 targets in Gaza, with one saying soldiers had about 20 seconds to review each target before they carried out a strike.
The U.S. has since made a major push to ramp up AI use, with the Pentagon declaring the country's military an "AI-first fighting force."

The U.S. used Anthropic's Claude chatbot to help identify nearly 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours of its war with Iran in February. After a U.S. missile strike on a girls' school in Minab, American senators raised concerns over the use of AI tools, including Palantir's Maven Smart System, in target selection.

Those concerns did not deter the military. In June, Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer for the department of defence, said Elon Musk's Grok chatbot had been used to launch thousands of missiles at Iran.
Why Canada’s military deal with Palantir sparks sovereignty fears

The frequency of AI-assisted targeting in Gaza and Iran has raised concerns from experts who worry that even though a human technically may have the final say before strikes are made, that human could effectively serve as a rubber stamp.
'Dystopian future'

Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws who teaches at Washburn University in Topeka, Kan, also worries about automation bias, whereby humans tend to become overly confident in AI's accuracy and validity.
"This may have been the case in the ... use of Lavender in Gaza, similarly the incident of the strike on the school in Minab by the United States," he told CBC News.
Craig Martin, a former Canadian navy officer and an expert in armed conflict laws, would like to see a ban on fully autonomous weapons. (Andrew Lee/CBC)
Martin is calling for changes to international law that would ban fully autonomous weapons and restrict semi-autonomous weapons.
He says he has hope for some form of agreement on AI, but it "would be a mistake to say that one is extremely optimistic," given that international law is in "a bit of a crisis right now."

"My greatest fear would be that we miss this window of opportunity and we increasingly develop weapons that are governed by AI over which we have little control and often little understanding and no legal regime that's governing those weapon systems," he said.
"It could lead to some kind of dystopian future."

items: NATO's race against time: Senior commander warns alliance must adapt faster to deter Russia
Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet

blocks.text: Lushenko says his concerns extend to nuclear weapons.

While noting that AI offers the possibility of built-in deterrents and has potential to reduce human error and civilian casualties, he says war games conducted in research programs have found AI chatbots tend to rapidly escalate to suggesting the use of nukes in evolving crises between powerful countries.
Fears of escalation

The fear among major powers of being left behind is driving a "race to the bottom," said Branka Marijan, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and senior researcher with anti-war organization Project Ploughshares.
"Without those guardrails we really, I think, are in a very dangerous moment," she said.

Branka Marijan, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and senior researcher with Project Ploughshares, says the world is in a 'dangerous moment' without guardrails around AI in war. (Submitted by Branka Marijan)

Marijan says what keeps her up at night is not necessarily the sheer destruction that could be caused by autonomous weapons or by AI selecting targets in the midst of an ongoing war, but mistakes that could cause an international incident to escalate into a full-blown crisis.
CNN reported in September that the U.S. military almost boarded a Chinese vessel in the Middle East because an AI chatbot mistakenly said the ship was carrying nuclear materials.
The Canadian company arming Ukraine with drones
Marijan says incidents like that "are likely to keep occurring" and next time, the military might not put the brakes on soon enough.
"You could have a system that completely influences a state actor to act in a way that might be based on faulty information ... that results in some catastrophic mistake."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kevin Maimann is a senior writer for CBC News based in Edmonton. He has covered a wide range of topics for publications including VICE, the Toronto Star, Xtra Magazine and the Edmonton Journal. You can reach Kevin by email at kevin.maimann@cbc.ca.
With files from Jennifer Yoon

articles.title: 2027 Grammy nominations release today. Here's what you need to know
articles.summary: Nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards are scheduled to be announced today, broadcast live from New York's Time Square on Grammy.com and the Grammys' YouTube channel.

image.caption: Nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards are scheduled to be announced today, broadcasting live from New York's Time Square on Grammy.com and the Grammys YouTube channel. (Robyn Beck/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards are scheduled to be announced today, broadcast live from New York's Time Square on Grammy.com and the Grammys' YouTube channel.
Nominations for 69th annual Grammy Awards to broadcast live at 7:45 a.m. ET
Nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards are scheduled to be announced today, broadcasting live from New York's Time Square on Grammy.com and the Grammys YouTube channel.

The annual honours will start at 7:45 a.m. ET before a wrap-up show at 9 a.m. ET, the latter of which will highlight select nominees. Scheduled presenters for the main show include Alan Menken, David Guetta, Linda Perry, Herbie Hancock, Olivia Dean, Pharrell Williams, Yungblud and Renée Fleming.
This year, the awards boast five new categories and brand new eligibility rules. Those changes will partially shape the slate of performers announced today, particularly in the new artist category.

There, artists are now allowed to submit for that category four times throughout their career instead of three; according to Billboard, that opens up the opportunity for potential front-runners Ella Langley and Megan Moroney, who otherwise would be ineligible this year.

Meanwhile, there are five entirely new categories this year: best Latin song, best traditional folk album, best traditional pop vocal performance, best R&B collaboration or duo/group performance and best Asian pop music performance. The last addition struck a sour note with some music fans and creators — particularly in the K-pop space.
BTS won’t enter the 2027 Grammy Awards
Controversial new category
A month after the Recording Academy, which organizes the Grammys, announced the new awards space, powerhouse group BTS shared a joint statement saying they would not submit their music.

“We hope our music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language,” the co-ordinated message read. “We thank [fanbase] Army and everyone who has always stood by us.”

Some fans viewed the new category as a racialized barrier for Asian performers — especially so soon after Golden from the film Kpop Demon Hunters became the first K-pop song to win a Grammy earlier this year. The Grammys caused similar controversy when they split up the country album category into "traditional" and "contemporary" after Beyoncé became the first Black artist to win best country album in 2025.

The new Latin song category also reflects the growing popularity of that genre. At the 68th Grammy Awards, Bad Bunny's DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS became the first all-Spanish release to win album of the year, the night's highest honour.

Today's nominations come shortly after the 27th annual Latin Grammy Awards, which saw Spanish singer Rosalía win album of the year on Thursday. The 69th Grammy Awards themselves will take place Feb. 7, 2027, on ABC and stream on Disney+ and Hulu, live from Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jackson Weaver is a reporter and film critic for CBC's entertainment news team in Toronto. You can reach him at jackson.weaver@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Canada presented itself as a global leader in methane reductions at COP31. But is Alberta holding it back?
articles.summary: Canada took centre stage at COP31 last week to showcase its track record on cutting methane emissions. But some experts say the country can't be a global leader on reducing methane until Alberta,…

image.caption: A section of the Syncrude oil sands facility near Fort McMurray, Alta., pictured on April 14. The oil and gas sector accounts for nearly half of Canada's methane emissions. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: After more than a year of fielding scathing critique from climate experts for rolling back climate policies and doubling down on fossil fuel projects, Canada took centre stage at COP31 last week to showcase its track record on cutting methane emissions.
But some experts say the federal government needs buy-in from Alberta before it can boast.

Canada has touted itself as a leader in the field, with Environment and Climate Change Canada calling efforts to minimize methane emissions “a clear near-term success story” ahead of last Wednesday's ministerial meeting in Antalya, Turkey, for the Global Methane Pledge, a coalition of 159 countries that Canada co-convenes with the European Union.

At the meeting, Canada pledged $10 million in funding to further global reductions of the potent greenhouse gas, and then on Friday announced a program that aims to connect Canadian businesses selling methane-reduction technology with interested buyers internationally, stating in a news release that it will "bring Canadian methane solutions to the world."

But some experts are pointing out that while Canada has made progress in cutting methane emissions and has strong federal regulations, it's still waiting for Alberta — the country’s biggest oil and gas producer — to bring its equivalent provincial regulations up to date.

And with emissions historically under-reported in Alberta, which relies on industry-reported data, experts are saying a stronger line needs to be taken at home before Canada can sell itself as a model to follow.

items: Canada's credibility on the line at COP31 as it defends fossil fuel expansion while trumpeting clean energy

blocks.text: The “job is sort of half-done,” according to Amanda Bryant, oil and gas analyst for the clean-energy think-tank the Pembina Institute.
“Real progress has been made on methane emissions in Canada, particularly in the oil and gas sector, and that's because of the regulatory approach that's been taken to date across Canada,” she said.
“But further progress really hinges on this federal government protecting the integrity of its own regulation and not kneecapping the strength of its regulation by being soft on Alberta.”
How Canada's methane regulations work

Methane is a heat-trapping greenhouse gas responsible for around a third of the rise in temperatures globally. Although it doesn’t linger as long in the atmosphere as carbon dioxide does, its impact is more than 80 times stronger over a 20-year period.
Methane is emitted by a variety of sources, including wetlands, landfills and livestock, but nearly half of Canada’s methane emissions — 48 per cent — come from the oil and gas sector.
Roughly 68 per cent of that comes from Alberta’s oil and gas sector, followed by 18 per cent from Saskatchewan and seven per cent from British Columbia, according to a 2024 study.
Environment minister announces new methane regulations

Because it is potent and can be repurposed as the main component in natural gas, countries have long seen reducing methane emissions as a quick, cost-effective way to cut greenhouse gases. According to the federal government, Canada is currently on track to reduce methane emissions by more than 35 per cent by 2030 compared to 2020 levels.
But the accuracy of this outlook depends on provincial regulations.

items: Youth, advocacy groups sue Carney government over climate rollbacks
Oil and gas emissions rising as other sectors mostly flat, federal data shows

blocks.text: Under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act (CEPA), provinces can opt out of federal regulations provided they present a regulatory plan that shows they can provide equivalent results on the same timeline.

The model has produced results in B.C., where, under an equivalency agreement put in place in 2020, the province roughly halved its methane emissions from oil and gas by 2023, surpassing its target reduction two years early, according to Canada’s 2025 National Inventory Report.

However, Alberta, B.C. and Saskatchewan have yet to finalize equivalency agreements that match the latest methane regulations outlined by the federal government in December 2025, which laid out a pathway for a 75 per cent reduction in the oil and gas sector from 2012 levels by 2030.
'The planet is not dying, it is being killed' - Thunberg at COP 31
Moreover, according to the memorandum of understanding the federal government signed with Alberta last fall, that province has actually been given longer to comply with the regulations.

As well as giving federal backing to a new oil pipeline and granting Alberta special exemptions from environmental laws, the MOU also laid out a requirement for the province to create a draft equivalency agreement, specifying a commitment of a 75 per cent reduction from 2014 levels by 2035 — an extension of the federal timeline that has confounded experts.

"Any kind of delay translates into more cumulative emissions," said Bryant. "If we're thinking about how to achieve a national target of 75 per cent by 2030 … it's not clear how giving Alberta more time adds up."
When asked by CBC News why Alberta was given a five-year-extension, Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) did not provide a reason.
"The approach to assessing equivalency in Alberta will remain consistent with the requirements of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act," said ECCC spokesperson Amy Falkner in a statement.

items: What's new in Ottawa-Alberta deal to cut methane emissions from oil and gas sector
Alberta, Ottawa reach 'agreement-in-principle' on methane emissions

blocks.text: In March, Alberta followed up on the MOU by signing an agreement in principle, which promised it would deliver its draft equivalency agreement in time for a 60-day public comment period and finalization by the end of 2026. With less than 50 days left in the year, this hasn’t materialized.

The updated federal regulations won't come into effect until January 2028. But the delay on Alberta's equivalency agreement has experts worried there will be a rush to approve inadequate provincial regulation, without public input, potentially leaving existing problems unaddressed.
"This works remains ongoing," Falkner said of the timeline, without providing further detail.
Alberta Environment Minister Grant Hunter, who was a speaker at a COP31 panel this week championing Canada’s methane reductions, did not respond to a request for comment.
Emissions under-reported in Alberta

One of the big updates in Alberta's agreement in principle is the requirement of independent, third-party verification of the province’s emissions — a crucial step forward considering multiple studies have found more methane is being emitted than is recorded in the province’s official statistics.

According to Alberta’s numbers, calculated using industry-reported estimates, methane emissions in 2023 had reduced by 52 per cent compared to 2014 levels — but the federal government, which also includes aerial measurements and independent research, has said the reduction was only 35 per cent.
Methane from abandoned oil wells worse than initially recorded
If provinces and the federal government don’t agree on a baseline for emissions, an agreement to reduce them isn’t going to produce equivalent results, Bryant noted.

“If someone promises you 75 per cent of a very small pizza or 75 per cent of a very large pizza, it really makes a difference, the sort of baseline size of the pizza, to how much pizza you're going to end up with,” she said.

items: Old, inactive oil and gas wells emitting almost 7 times more methane than official estimates
Wildfires, permafrost thaw in Canada causing even more climate change, new study shows

blocks.text: Until the new equivalency agreement is approved, Alberta continues to operate under its existing agreement on methane regulations, which was only designed to achieve a 40 to 45 per cent reduction in methane emissions from 2012 levels by 2025.

Additionally, Alberta currently has no regulations over intentional venting of methane into the atmosphere, which is prohibited federally except in rare circumstances. Federal rules also require more frequent leak checks at high-risk sites than Alberta does, and prohibits routine flaring, a practice of burning off excess gas during oil production, which the province doesn’t ban.
“There are some major gaps between these sets of regulations and some real work for Alberta to do,” Bryant said.
A 'good news story' to deflect climate criticism?

Canada’s performance at COP31 comes at a time when the federal government is under serious scrutiny for backtracking on climate policies and ignoring the scientific consensus that new fossil fuel investments are incompatible with keeping global temperatures down.
A group of youth climate activists are even suing the government for not doing enough to fight climate change.
Are Canada’s climate plans cooked?

Robb Barnes, climate program director with the Canadian Association of Physicians for the Environment, noted Canada's climate reversal includes the Carney government scrapping a promised oil and gas emissions cap, backtracking on industrial and consumer carbon pricing and rollbacks of the EV mandate.
He said methane is one area the government has been keen to point to, possibly as a "good news story" to deflect criticism while on the world stage.

items: 'Just stop burning fossil fuels.' Scientists stress our smoky skies have only one true fix
Leading climate think-tank says Canada won't meet 2030 climate target

blocks.text: But amid claims of its perceived special treatment of Alberta, Barnes noted it's on the federal government to apply the necessary pressure if it wants to live up to its methane boasts.
“The equivalency agreements are negotiations between the province and the federal government,” he said. “So there’s lack of political will in many places, if you know where to look.”

articles.title: Montreal students reeling from police violence at Nov. 13 education austerity protest
articles.summary: Montreal students are denouncing the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) for what they call unjustified acts of violence during a protest against education austerity that took place on…

image.caption: None of the protesters CBC News interviewed said they were told to leave the site of the Nov. 13 student protest before Montreal police deployed tear gas. (CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal students are denouncing the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) for what they call unjustified acts of violence during a protest against education austerity that took place on Friday.

The Nov. 13 protest was organized by the Coalition de résistance pour l'unité étudiante syndicale (CRUES), which called on the province to reform its student financial assistance program and increase funding for CEGEPs and universities.

While protesters in attendance described the mood in Victoria Square, where they first gathered, as originally festive and joyous, there was a shift as the group of roughly 200 people began their procession into the streets.

An SPVM spokesperson said that a demonstrator started to commit mischief, breaking a window and damaging a vehicle, which led to the protest being declared illegal. According to police, a firework was also fired at an officer by that one demonstrator.
"We had to deploy tear gas to spread the crowd that was aggressive at that time," said Bergeron.

Police say two people were arrested for armed assault on a police officer and another was arrested for assault on a police officer. Police noted eight incidents of mischief involving buildings or vehicles, but no citizen injuries.
'It made me feel a bit of despair for humanity'
Maxim Lepage, a 20-year-old psychoeducation student at the Université de Montréal, remembers the events of the protest differently.
She said she received no verbal warning from police to disperse, and only knew something had gone wrong after tear gas starting hitting the crowd.

She said that the people she was protesting with ran into a side street to flee from an advancing group of roughly 30 officers. Lepage was running away on St-Dominique Street when she turned around, and says she saw a man alone on the ground, surrounded by officers who were kicking him.

items: Montreal police use tear gas to disperse downtown student protest

blocks.text: Lepage said that when she and her friend turned around to address the officers, her friend was hit in the throat with a police riot shield. Lepage then said she was hit in the face with another officer's shield, causing her nose to begin bleeding.
Maxim Lepage says she was hit in the face by a police officer's riot shield during the Nov. 13 student protest. (Submitted by William Wilson)

It turned out to be broken. Lepage was given first-aid support by paramedics at the protest, before going to the Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM) in a taxi, and waiting for 15 hours to be treated. A friend of Lepage's suspected she might have a concussion, and also waited there for eight hours, before ultimately leaving untreated.

Lepage waited 15 hours in the emergency room at the Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM) with a broken nose. There, she saw three other injured protesters from the Nov. 13 demonstration. (Submitted by Maxim Lepage)
Lepage says she also saw two other protesters at the hospital waiting for medical attention: one who had hurt their leg, and another who had received a projectile to the face.
Urgences-santé said that three people from the protest were transported by ambulance to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and that one person refused transport.
"It was pretty shocking to see a group from the protest in the emergency room," said Lepage. "It made me feel a bit of despair for humanity."
'Easily the most terrifying seconds of my life'

Mere feet away from Lepage in the emergency room was Rebecca Mota, an 18-year-old CEGEP student from Collège de Maisonneuve. She was the protester with the injured leg, needing X-rays for a potential fracture, and getting referred to another doctor for tenderness in her abdomen.

A member of her school's student association, Mota had encouraged a number of friends, who had not participated in any protests before, to attend the demonstration with her. She had been expecting it to go peacefully.
"No one was prepared for the way it was going to go," said Mota. "They threw so much gas in such little time."

Like Lepage, Mota also recalled the tear gas coming without warning. Mota and her friends began to run away, but kept being caught up to by police. Eventually, amid the chaos, she fell to the ground and couldn't get back up.
"The police pushed someone, and that person fell on me," said Mota. "Despite the fact that we were still on the floor and that we couldn't get up, the police would still push us with their shields."
"It was horrible, the time I spent on the floor was easily the most terrifying seconds of my life."
Then, Mota remembered not being able to leave, despite wanting to, because the protesters were surrounded by officers.
Both she and Lepage had come to the protest initially to draw attention to the circumstances of austerity facing their education system.

items: Striking Quebec students prepared to escalate push for better education funding
Quebec assumes parents help pay for post-secondary schooling. Students say many can't

blocks.text: Mota says knows fellow students who work 20-hour weeks while studying for another 30 in class, not including time spent on homework. She says that they live in economic precarity, and that the support their schools offer is lacking.
Lepage, for her part, says she has worked over 400 unpaid hours for her university internship, on top of holding down a job and studying, and that she has regularly skipped meals to get by.
For her, the protest was to show that youth have a voice, to exercise her democratic rights, and to get the attention of the provincial government.
Instead, she said, "it just showed at what point the government was badly doing its job."

"I was really hoping that the protest would be a way for students from so many schools to get together and show that we all care about this issue," said Mota. "For so many people, it was their first experience [at a protest], and they got attacked."
Police repression historically harder on students, say advocates

Laurence Guénette, the coordinator and spokesperson for the Ligue des droits et libertés (LDL), said that her organization has received several photos documenting injuries students received at the protest at the hands of the police.

"The testimonies we have really question the narrative of clashes taking place between the demonstrators and the police," said Guénette. "It's more like the brutality of the police repression is absolutely unacceptable."
She said multiple people who ran away from the police during the dispersal operation were "strongly hit."

While shocked, she said that the LDL is not surprised, given the police have historically been harder on students during other periods of protest against educational conditions, namely strikes against tuition raises in 2012.
Karine Cliche, a professor from CEGEP Montmorency who was present on Friday, also participated in student protests during the 2012 strikes.
"This protest, it's the first time I saw a repression that was so fast to stop a peaceful movement and a legitimate cause of protest," she said.
The protest took place on Friday and began at around 2 p.m. Square-Victoria in downtown Montreal. (Philippe Robitaille-Grou/Radio-Canada)
Cliche says police pepper sprayed her multiple times while she was at the front lines of the protest.
Québec Solidaire MNA Gisèle Pouhe Njall showed up to the protest to show her support for students. She witnessed a young man being beaten by officers after falling down of his own accord.
"He didn't mean any wrong, he just happened to fall," she said. "He tried to step back up, and I saw with my own eyes police officers going to him and beating him."

items: Montreal police chief defends push to change SPVM culture, weed out bad apples
'He targeted me': Journalist says he was beaten by Montreal police at anti-AI protest

blocks.text: Pouhe Njall said she was also afraid when people next to her were hit by police with shields.
None of the protesters CBC News interviewed said that they heard a verbal notice to leave the protest before tear gas was deployed.
The SPVM and the mayor's office did not respond in time for publication to a request for comment on the allegations of abuse made by protesters against officers during the dispersal operation.
'We stopped talking about the students' demands'

Following the protest, Elsie Lefebvre, the minister of higher education, and Guy Lapointe Jr., the domestic security minister, posted the same message on X, stating that the government recognizes students' right to protest, but that they condemned acts of violence and vandalism from protesters during the demonstration that put those peacefully gathering at risk.
Pouhe Njall called on Lefebvre to meet with students to address their concerns directly.

"What I absolutely find scary is that we stopped talking about the students' demands," she said. "The cost of living is so high that our students in Quebec cannot go to school, have an internship, study at the same time, eat and have a full belly and a roof over their heads."
"Unfortunately, we've lost track of that, with what happened yesterday."
The student mobilization could continue into the winter semester, with student associations expected to vote later this month on whether to call an unlimited general strike.
For their part, Lepage and Mota said that Friday's events did not dim their desire to have their voices heard.
"It makes me want to protest more," said Lepage.

articles.title: UK and allies call on Israel to allow rapid humanitarian access to Gaza
articles.summary: The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy say Israeli authorities are holding back vital supplies at the borders, including 150,00 tents.

blocks.text: The UK, Australia, Canada and Italy have issued a joint statement urging Israel to "allow immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout Gaza", where they say the situation on the ground is "dire".
The foreign ministers warn recent floods have brought "further suffering" to the war-torn territory, which recently had its first winter storm.
The statement says 150,000 tents and other vital supplies are being held at the border.

The Israeli military authority which controls the Gaza crossings has said it is co-ordinating with the US-led Board of Peace and the UN on a winter plan, and that 93,000 tents and 8,600 aid trucks with winter supplies had entered the territory.
It added that reconstruction "can only begin after Hamas fully disarms".

The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs said the widespread flooding and a landslide led to a number of deaths, thousands of damaged shelters and the suspension of critical services.

The statement from the British, Australian, Canadian and Italian foreign ministers says, external: "This situation is entirely reversible - and there is still time to act before the winter fully sets in."
"The crossings must be opened, and the tents allowed in. Dual-use items necessary for humanitarian operations and early recovery must be granted entry before it is too late."
The European Union issued a similar statement on Saturday, external, reiterating its "grave concern" over what it called the "persistent and devastating humanitarian crisis".
The EU also urged Israel to comply with international law.
The war in Gaza was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 74,690 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israeli air strikes and other attacks have continued to take place almost every day despite the ceasefire agreed in October last year.
